fields.description:
# J11 — Prove bidirectional reconciliation live, against a realistic store

## Why this exists

Epic e369's headline AC is:

> [operator-attested] rebar reconciles bidirectionally against the Dockerized Jira instance ... at
> least one issue created in DC appears in the local store after an inbound pass, and one local edit
> appears on the DC issue after an outbound pass, with zero unhandled exceptions

It is NOT met, and the way it failed is instructive. CI run 30637886718 reported:

    invariants: scanned=0 filed=0
    OK: steady-state pass converged
    RECON: outbound_differ total=0   inbound_differ total=0

**Scanned zero.** The pass converged because there was nothing to reconcile. That proves the
reconciler runs cleanly against an EMPTY instance — it does not prove data moves. On an empty store
'converged' and 'works' are indistinguishable, and only one of them is the criterion. Closing the epic
on that output would have been the fifth instance in this epic of green-but-broken.

The existing live module builds its store with the `rebar_repo` fixture: `rebar.init_repo()` on an
empty temp dir. Nothing to sync, so nothing syncs.

## Approach

Run the live verification against a COPY OF THIS PROJECT'S ACTUAL TICKET STORE, so the pass sees
realistic volume, ticket shapes, link graphs, comment histories and field values — the conditions that
surface ordering and field-mapping defects an empty store cannot.
(Deliberately NOT "pagination": that is a property of the REMOTE issue count, not of the local store,
and is exercised by seeding the harness — see the volume bullet below. An earlier draft listed it here
and contradicted that bullet.)

### Isolation is the first requirement, not an afterthought

rebar AUTO-COMMITS and AUTO-PUSHES ticket events to `sync.remote`. A copy of this project's store that
retained its configuration could push test mutations back at the real project. Defence in depth, in
priority order:

1. **A SEPARATE REPO WITH NO REMOTES — the primary mechanism.** The CI job `git init`s a fresh repo
   and copies the ticket-store content in. It never adds `origin`, so there is physically
   nowhere to push, independent of any config or env value. This is stronger than a flag
   because it cannot be defeated by a mis-read setting.
   **HOW the content is obtained, because it is NOT in a normal checkout:** `.tickets-tracker/` is
   GITIGNORED (`.gitignore:9`) and the store lives on the ORPHAN `tickets` branch, which
   `actions/checkout` does not fetch. The job must explicitly `git fetch origin tickets` in the
   SOURCE checkout and materialise that tree, then `git init` + commit it in the destination.
   Copying the workspace directory would copy nothing.
   **EXTRACT INTO `.tickets-tracker/`, NOT INTO THE REPO ROOT — an earlier draft's command was
   wrong and would have produced a store the reconciler cannot see.** The orphan `tickets` branch
   holds the ticket files AND `.bridge_state` at ITS OWN ROOT (`git ls-tree origin/tickets` shows
   `.bridge_state`, `.store-compat.json`, and bare ticket-id entries such as `003a-09ae-9983-4007`),
   whereas the reconciler reads `tracker_dir = repo_root / ".tickets-tracker"` (`reconcile.py:265`).
   Extracting to the root therefore lands every ticket one directory ABOVE where the pass looks,
   so the pass sees NO LOCAL TICKETS — a store that is empty as far as the reconciler is
   concerned, reproduced by the setup rather than by the product. (Note this does NOT surface as
   `scanned=0`: that number counts REMOTE Jira issues, not local tickets — see the store-copy AC.
   It is caught by the ticket-count check, which is why that check reads the filesystem.)
   The command is:
       mkdir -p <fresh repo>/.tickets-tracker
       git archive FETCH_HEAD | tar -x -C <fresh repo>/.tickets-tracker
   and the fixture must ASSERT the layout after extraction (ticket files exist under
   `.tickets-tracker/`) rather than trust the redirection.
   **THE WORKING REPO ALSO NEEDS A CONFIG, and it has none — it is a fresh `git init`.** The copied
   tree carries tickets, not reconciler settings, so the fixture must WRITE a `rebar.toml` into the
   fresh repo containing `[reconciler]` with `base_url = "http://localhost:2990/jira"` (plus the
   project key and `allow_insecure = true`, since the harness serves plain http). That written file is
   also what the `base_url` AC below inspects — the check and the setup must name the same file, or
   the check passes by finding nothing.
2. `REBAR_SYNC_PUSH=off` as a second, independent layer (`sync.push` accepts `always|async|off`;
   the env override is authoritative).
   **Do NOT assert on `sync.remote`.** It defaults to `"origin"` (`_config_schema.py:307`) whether or
   not such a remote exists, so "sync.remote is empty" is neither achievable nor meaningful — and
   setting it empty to satisfy a check would give false confidence while changing nothing. The
   assertion that carries real weight is that `git remote` in the working repo returns NOTHING.
3. The reconciler config points ONLY at the harness (`reconciler.base_url` = the container). No Cloud
   credentials are present in the job environment at all — no `JIRA_URL`, no `JIRA_API_TOKEN`, no
   `acli` auth — so the Cloud path cannot be driven even by accident.
4. **The isolation is ASSERTED, not assumed.** A test fails the job if `git remote` returns anything in
   the working repo. (NOT on `sync.remote` — see layer 2: it defaults to `"origin"` regardless, so
   that assertion can never pass and would only invite someone to weaken it.) Safety that is not
   tested is an intention.

### The copy must be SCRUBBED of Jira IDs and reconciler artifacts

Isolation stops ticket events ESCAPING. It does not stop the reconciler forming an intent to WRITE to
a production issue key. The scrub is an independent layer and both are required.

Enumerated against this project's REAL tickets branch, not assumed:

    .bridge_state/bindings.json
    .bridge_state/bindings-retired.json
    .bridge_state/prev_snapshot.json
    .bridge_state.bak-retarget/bindings.json
    .bridge_state.bak-retarget/prev_snapshot.json

Two traps a naive scrub falls into:

* **`.bridge_state.bak-retarget/` also holds real bindings.** It is a backup left by a past project
  retarget. Deleting `.bridge_state/` by name removes the live set and leaves a SECOND full set of
  production Jira bindings in the copy. Match the pattern `.bridge_state*`, and assert none survive —
  do not delete a hardcoded list. The existence of this directory is itself proof that the artifact
  set drifts over time, so the scrub must ENUMERATE the copied tree.
* **`prev_snapshot.json` must still be scrubbed — but it is NOT detectable from mutation counts,
  and two earlier drafts of this plan got that wrong in opposite directions.** It is the OUTBOUND
  field-change baseline (`OutboundDiffConfig.prev_snapshot`, consumed in
  `outbound_differ.compute_outbound_mutations`), NOT an inbound create/delete trigger: the inbound
  and legacy differs decide creates from the CURRENT snapshot. So a leftover production copy does
  not drive mass DELETION — that much an earlier draft got right.
  What that draft then got WRONG is the claim that it produces a wave of spurious outbound UPDATEs
  that the run can detect. It cannot, and the reason is mechanical: `outbound_differ.py:518-520`
  branches on `binding_store.get_jira_key(local_id)`, and `None` routes to the CREATE path — an
  UPDATE is only ever emitted for a ticket that HAS a binding. The scrub removes `bindings.json`,
  so no ticket has one, so a `prev_snapshot.json` surviving ON ITS OWN emits nothing at all.
  **Therefore it is caught DIRECTLY, by the scrub-completeness criterion asserting `.bridge_state*`
  is absent — an observation of the file itself, not an inference from mutation counts.** See the
  zero-counts AC for the full derivation; this bullet and that AC must agree, and an earlier
  revision left them contradicting each other.

### The DC-side mutation suite

Comprehensive mutations applied to the HARNESS instance (never a real Jira), each asserted to
round-trip against a NAMED per-mutation oracle (the table in the acceptance criteria gives the
proving read for every cell), so the bridge is exercised rather than merely started. The ONE
exception is `set_parent`'s epic case, which by design does not round-trip and is asserted
directly against the transport — stated here as well as in the ACs so the two cannot drift:

* **inbound (DC -> local), fourteen mutations:** create issue; edit summary; edit description;
  transition status; add label; remove label; add comment; assign; unassign; create issue link;
  delete issue link; set sub-task parent; clear parent; delete issue (absence probe).
  **`edit comment` is deliberately NOT in this list.** An earlier draft required it in both
  directions. The reconciler has no edit-comment mutation type and `JiraDataCenterTransport` has no
  `update_comment`, so it specified a capability that does not exist. If comment editing is wanted it
  is a separate feature story, not a verification criterion.
* **outbound (local -> DC), enumerated rather than described as "the mirror set":** create ticket ->
  issue; edit title -> summary; edit description; transition status; add label; remove label; add
  comment; set assignee; clear assignee; create link; delete link; set parent; clear parent; delete
  ticket. Fourteen, matching the inbound list one-for-one — `set_parent`'s epic case is expected to
  raise `NotImplementedError` (see bda8's triage), asserted **directly against the transport**
  (`with pytest.raises(NotImplementedError): transport.set_parent(...)`), NOT through the reconciler
  subprocess. `dispatch_one._update_one_apply_parent` catches `Exception` (dispatch_one.py:564) and
  only logs, so the exception is SWALLOWED inside a pass: no traceback, unchanged return code, and
  therefore indistinguishable on the subprocess streams from a mutation that succeeded. Routing that
  assertion through the subprocess would make it untestable by construction — the same
  swallowed-exception trap that let J9's twelve missing members pass 1600 tests.
* **volume — and note WHAT drives it.** Pagination is a property of the REMOTE issue count, not of
  the local store copy. The store copy buys realistic local volume, ticket shapes and link graphs;
  it does NOT exercise paging at all. To exercise paging the suite must CREATE issues in the harness.
  Procedure, because guessing the cap is how truncation stays hidden: first READ the instance's
  effective page size (issue a `search_issues` with a high `maxResults` and observe what the server
  actually returns — Jira 8.17.1 defaults to 50, but `jira.search.views.default.max` is
  server-configurable and the server silently truncates), then seed at least `2 * observed + 1`
  issues so at least three pages are required. Assert the observed cap in the test output so a
  future instance change is visible rather than silent.
* **idempotence:** an immediately repeated pass after each direction writes nothing.

### Sequence: a thin slice BEFORE the comprehensive suite

The riskiest unknown is not any individual mutation — it is whether the copied-and-scrubbed store
drives a live pass at all. So land a vertical slice first: fetch + scrub + isolation assertions, ONE
inbound round-trip (create in DC, assert it appears locally) and ONE outbound round-trip (edit
locally, assert it appears in DC). Only once that is green in CI does the full mutation suite go in.
Building all thirteen mutations against an unproven harness path risks debugging thirteen failures
that share one root cause.

## Scope

- `.github/workflows/external-integration.yml` — the `jira-dc-harness` job gains the store-copy step
  (fresh `git init`, no remote) and the isolation assertions.
- `tests/external/live_jira_dc/` — the mutation suite and its fixtures; a `dc_mutations` helper that
  applies each DC-side change through the real transport.
- `tests/external/live_jira_dc/README.md` — document the isolation contract and WHY (auto-push).

**NOT in scope:** any change that could write to this project's Jira or its tickets branch.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] the working repo in CI has NO git remote, asserted by a test that FAILS the job otherwise —
      this is the primary isolation and it must be verified, not assumed
- [ ] `REBAR_SYNC_PUSH=off` is asserted in the same test as the no-remote check
- [ ] no Cloud credential is present in the job environment, asserted by test
- [ ] the store under test is a COPY of this project's real ticket store, proved by COUNTING
      LOCAL TICKETS DIRECTLY — not by the pass's `scanned` number.
      **THIS AC PREVIOUSLY MEASURED THE WRONG SIDE OF THE BRIDGE, and correcting it also corrects
      this epic's founding diagnosis.** `scanned` is `len(curr_snapshot)` (`run_differs.py:282`),
      and `curr_snapshot` is `fetcher.compute_snapshot(...)` (`reconcile.py:286`) — the normalized
      **JIRA** snapshot, i.e. the count of REMOTE issues fetched from the harness. It says nothing
      whatever about how many LOCAL tickets the copied store holds. The isolated harness starts
      with no issues, so a pass run before any DC seeding reports zero no matter how large the copy
      is; the old AC would have failed on a perfectly good store, and could never have proved the
      thing it was written to prove.
      This also means the epic's original reading of the earlier failing run was wrong. That run's
      `scanned=0` was recorded (handoff #4) as "it converged because the STORE was EMPTY". On this
      code it means the HARNESS had no issues — a remote-side fact. The local store may well have
      been fine. The conclusion drawn from it (that a pass over an empty input proves nothing)
      still stands; the mechanism attributed to it does not.
      **THE CORRECT OBSERVABLE — count the copy, on the filesystem, before any pass runs.** Assert
      that the number of ticket entries under `<working repo>/.tickets-tracker/` equals the number
      on the fetched `tickets` branch (`git ls-tree --name-only FETCH_HEAD`, excluding the dot-files
      `.bridge_state*`, `.gitattributes`, `.gitignore`, `.store-compat.json`, `.ticket-write.lock`),
      and that it is > 0. Comparing the two counts rather than asserting a bare floor is what makes
      this catch a PARTIAL extraction, which a `> 0` check would wave through.
      Keep the remote-side number too, but label it honestly: after the pagination cells seed the
      harness, the same line reports how many issues the fetch actually saw, and that is the
      truncation signal the seeding criterion already owns. Where to read it, since it is not in the
      JSON envelope and two earlier revisions of this AC got the stream and the wording wrong:
      `run_differs.py:270-283` branches on
      `skip_invariant_filing = (not persist) or bool(filter_local_ids)`:
        * DRY-RUN takes the SKIP branch — `persist` is False because `MODE_CAPS[DRY_RUN] == 0`
          (`reconcile.py:218-222`) — and prints to STDERR (so no-write mode keeps STDOUT a pure
          JSON payload):
              invariants: skipped (no-write mode, <N> issues in snapshot)
          There is NO `scanned=` line in this mode at all.
        * A FILTERED pass — what the mutation cells use — hits the SAME skip branch (the gate is
          `(not persist) or bool(filter_local_ids)`) and prints
          `invariants: skipped (filtered pass, <N> issues in snapshot)` to STDERR.
        * The `scanned=<N> filed=<M> (cap=5)` line on STDOUT is emitted ONLY by an UNFILTERED
          WRITING pass — which this plan never runs (see the scoping note: unfiltered passes are
          dry-run only). It is documented here so a future reader does not go looking for that
          line in this suite's output and conclude something is broken when it is simply absent.
      Do not read `.scanned` from the envelope; there is no such key. The sibling `filed` counts
      INVARIANT-VIOLATION tickets, not tickets filed from DC issues, so `filed=0` is not evidence
      about inbound either way.
- [ ] the scrub matches `.bridge_state*` as a GLOB and a test asserts ZERO binding or snapshot
      artifacts survive anywhere in the copied tree — derived by enumerating the tree, not from a
      hardcoded list
- [ ] a test asserts the `.bridge_state*` scrub is COMPLETE — nothing matching `.bridge_state*`
      survives anywhere under the copied tracker dir, so a partially-scrubbed tree fails the job.
      NOT "the copied store holds no production Jira key reference", which an earlier draft required
      and which is MECHANICALLY UNACHIEVABLE: ticket event files under `.tickets-tracker/`
      legitimately embed `jira_key` values from prior Cloud syncs, the scrub correctly leaves that
      historical data intact (only BINDINGS drive remote writes — `binding_store.py:113`), so a
      whole-tree scan for production keys would ALWAYS hit and could never pass
- [ ] the first pass plans EXACTLY ZERO deletion mutations AND EXACTLY ZERO outbound UPDATE
      mutations, both read from the `--mode dry-run` JSON envelope on stdout (the no-write branch at
      `__main__.py:445-452` is the one that emits JSON; writing modes emit only an `OK:` line, so
      dry-run is what makes these counts observable at all).
      **THE EXACT KEYS, so the assertion needs no guesswork.** The envelope is the whole result
      dict (`reconcile.py:690-709`). The per-mutation plan is the top-level `plan` array, built by
      `_build_plan_entries` (`reconcile_helpers.py:450-480`), whose entries are exactly
      `{direction, action, target, local_id}`. `direction` is `MutationDirection` (`"inbound"` |
      `"outbound"`) and `action` is `MutationAction` (`"create"` | `"update"` | `"delete"` |
      `"probe"` | `"clean_label"` | `"repair_property"` | `"conflict"`) — both `StrEnum`, so they
      serialize as those literal strings (`mutation.py:17-29`). The two assertions are therefore:
          jq -e '[.plan[] | select(.action == "delete")] | length == 0'
          jq -e '[.plan[] | select(.direction == "outbound" and .action == "update")] | length == 0'
      Read the envelope from STDOUT ONLY: the human-readable `OK: dry-run computed …` line goes to
      STDERR precisely so it cannot corrupt the JSON, so the test must not merge the two streams.
      **BOTH COUNTS ARE ZERO, and an earlier draft's rationale for a non-zero tolerance was
      MECHANICALLY WRONG — corrected here from the code rather than softened.** That draft said
      `< 10` outbound UPDATEs independently detects a surviving `prev_snapshot.json` while the
      deletion count stays at a reassuring zero. It cannot. `outbound_differ.py:518-520` branches
      on `binding_store.get_jira_key(local_id)`: `None` routes to the CREATE path, so an UPDATE is
      only ever emitted for a ticket that HAS a binding. The scrub removes `bindings.json`, so no
      ticket has one, so a `prev_snapshot.json` that survives on its own produces NO outbound
      updates whatsoever — the assertion it was supposed to catch that failure with is blind to it.
      What the two assertions actually do:
        * ZERO deletions catches a surviving `bindings.json` — its production keys do not exist in
          the harness, so every bound ticket looks remotely deleted. This is the load-bearing one.
        * ZERO outbound updates is a SUBORDINATE guard on the same failure, for the case where a
          surviving binding's key happens to resolve in the harness. It is not an independent
          detector and must not be described as one.
      A surviving `prev_snapshot.json` is caught DIRECTLY instead, by the scrub-completeness
      criterion that asserts `.bridge_state*` is absent — an observation of the file, not an
      inference from mutation counts. Both counts are therefore exactly 0: with no bindings there
      is no legitimate source of either, and any non-zero value means the scrub failed.
- [ ] [operator-attested] an issue created in DC appears in the local store after an inbound pass.
      **The oracle for this is already FIXED and PROVEN, which an earlier draft did not record.**
      [rebar:23ed-de0a-765b-49aa] is CLOSED: the test had grepped the RAW Jira key against a payload
      whose id is the lowercased `jira-<key>` form and which carries no raw key at all, so it could
      never pass. It now matches by exact id via `_jira_key_to_local_id(remote_key)` AND asserts the
      binding store. EVIDENCE: CI run 30662366152, job "jira DC harness smoke",
      `test_a_dc_created_ticket_carries_the_shared_jira_provenance` PASSED in a fully green
      17-passed/0-skipped run. So this criterion is satisfiable today; it is the OUTBOUND half below
      that still has no evidence
- [ ] [operator-attested] a local edit appears on the DC issue after an outbound pass.
      THIS is the epic's unproven half and the reason this story exists: `test_reconcile_pass.py`
      has three live tests and NONE mutates a local ticket then asserts the change surfaces on the
      DC issue
- [ ] inbound DC assignee mutations MINT AN IDENTITY SUCCESSFULLY — asserted positively (the
      identity exists and carries the jira family), NOT merely that no exception escaped.
      **THE OBSERVABLE, since the identity is not a field on the ticket JSON.** After the inbound
      pass, call `rebar.ensure_identity_for("jira", <dc_user_name>, <display_name>)` — it is
      documented idempotent (resolve-or-mint, reusing an existing mapping) — and assert BOTH:
        (a) the id it returns EQUALS the local ticket's `.assignee` from `rebar show`, which is
            what proves the pass itself minted and attached the identity rather than the test
            creating one after the fact; and
        (b) the provider argument that satisfies (a) is the FAMILY string `"jira"`, not the
            deployment string `"jira-datacenter"` — that distinction IS bug 5f48, whose fix
            routes through `_identity_provider_for` asking the backend for `identity_family`
            (`apply_inbound_records.py:50-80`), because the store vocabulary is per-family.
      Assert on `<dc_user_name>` (Jira DC's `name`), not `accountId`: DC has no accountId at all,
      and the accountId-only guard is precisely what made 5f48 silent.
      **WHICH USER, resolved at runtime rather than hardcoded.** Take the assignee from
      `GET /rest/api/2/myself` on the harness — it returns the authenticated account's `name` and
      `displayName`, which are exactly the two values the assertion needs, and it cannot drift
      from whatever account the harness actually provisions (the compose default is `admin`, but
      reading it is what keeps this cell correct if that changes). Assign to that user and assert
      against the same pair.
      [rebar:5f48-244c-7063-42d0] is CLOSED and its fix is on `main` in commit 36e134401 ("b4e3:
      mint DC inbound identities as jira family", whose message records "Folds in bug 5f48"): the
      guard reads `for key in ("accountId", "name")` and `_identity_provider_for` asks the backend
      for `identity_family`. It was a SILENT failure — a swallowed `ValueError` degrading assignee
      resolution on every DC pass — and a no-exception assertion would have passed throughout it,
      which is exactly why this AC must assert the positive outcome
- [ ] every mutation in the suite above round-trips and is asserted INDIVIDUALLY (never by an
      aggregate 'converged' line), against the named observable below — EXCEPT `set_parent`'s
      epic case, which does NOT round-trip and is asserted directly against the transport with
      `pytest.raises(NotImplementedError)`. That carve-out is not an exemption: routing it
      through the reconciler would make it untestable by construction, because
      `dispatch_one._update_one_apply_parent` catches `Exception` (dispatch_one.py:564) and only
      logs, so a swallowed failure is indistinguishable from success on the subprocess streams.
      **THE ORACLE FOR EACH MUTATION — the proving read, so no cell is left to the executor's
      judgement.** Inbound cells mutate via the DC REST API, run an inbound pass, then read the
      LOCAL ticket as JSON (`rebar show <local_id>`); outbound cells mutate locally, run an
      outbound pass, then read the DC issue (`GET /rest/api/2/issue/{key}`). Each cell asserts
      the named path equals the value it wrote — not merely that the pass exited 0.

      | # | mutation | inbound oracle (path on `rebar show` JSON) | outbound oracle (path on the Jira issue) |
      |---|---|---|---|
      | 1 | create | a ticket exists at `_jira_key_to_local_id(key)` AND the binding store maps it | issue exists carrying label `rebar-id:<local_id>` (in `fields.labels`) AND entity property `local_id` read by RAW REST — `GET /rest/api/2/issue/{key}/properties/local_id` — because `JiraDataCenterTransport` has `set_entity_property` (transport.py:672) but NO getter, so this assertion is not reachable through the transport and must go direct |
      | 2 | edit summary/title | `.title` | `fields.summary` |
      | 3 | edit description | `.description` | `fields.description` |
      | 4 | transition status | `.status` | `fields.status.name` |
      | 5 | add label | `.tags` CONTAINS it | `fields.labels` CONTAINS it |
      | 6 | remove label | `.tags` does NOT contain it | `fields.labels` does NOT contain it |
      | 7 | add comment | some `.comments[].body` contains the text | some `fields.comment.comments[].body` contains it |
      | 8 | assign | `.assignee` is the mapped identity | `fields.assignee` names the mapped user |
      | 9 | unassign | `.assignee` is empty | `fields.assignee` is null |
      | 10 | create link | the link appears with the expected relation | `fields.issuelinks` contains the pair with that type |
      | 11 | delete link | that link is ABSENT | `fields.issuelinks` no longer contains it |
      | 12 | set parent | `.parent_id` is the parent's local id | sub-task case: `fields.parent.key`; EPIC case: the instance-discovered 'Epic Link' custom field, read back by RAW REST (no transport getter). AMENDED by operator ruling: the original text prescribed `pytest.raises(NotImplementedError)`, which [rebar:39c1-2a32-b564-4b4b] inverts by making the epic case WRITE the Epic Link — the AC would otherwise forbid the fix 39c1 exists to deliver. Coverage INCREASES (a real round-trip replaces an exception-type assertion); the carve-out's original justification is preserved, since the cell still asserts against the transport plus a raw-REST read-back rather than through a pass, because dispatch_one still swallows the exception. |
      | 13 | clear parent | `.parent_id` is null | `fields.parent` is absent |
      | 14 | delete (absence probe) | the dry-run plan contains an (inbound, probe) entry targeting the deleted key: `jq -e '[.plan[] \| select(.direction == "inbound" and .action == "probe" and .target == "<KEY>")] \| length == 1'` — see the REQUIRED SEQUENCING note below, without which this entry is never emitted | the issue is unreachable by key AND by numeric id (the 7c26 pair), so a deletion is not masked by a re-key |

      Rows 2-13 assert a value the cell itself wrote, so each is a genuine round-trip rather
      than a re-read of an unchanged field. Row 1 and row 14 are the two ends and are asserted
      structurally, since there is no prior/after value to compare.

      **SCOPE EVERY MUTATION PASS WITH `--filter-local-ids`, OR IT WILL TRY TO CREATE THE WHOLE
      STORE COPY IN DC.** This falls straight out of the branch below: after the scrub NO ticket
      has a binding, so an UNSCOPED outbound pass routes EVERY ticket in the copied store — the
      real project's, order 10^3 of them — down the CREATE path and attempts to file each one as a
      new DC issue. That would swamp the harness, take the run far past any sane budget, and
      destroy the very isolation this story is built to prove. `--filter-local-ids <local_id>`
      (`__main__.py:520`, parsed at `:680-689`) scopes the pass to the cell's own ticket, so each
      cell touches exactly the one ticket it is asserting about. Two consequences to carry:
        * UNFILTERED passes are permitted in exactly TWO places, both DRY-RUN and therefore
          incapable of writing: the scrub-verification pass, and the pagination-recovery pass
          (which MUST be unfiltered — a filtered pass never crosses a page boundary and so
          cannot test paging at all). No unfiltered WRITING pass is ever run.
          (The store-copy check is a filesystem ticket
          count, not a pass at all, so it needs no scoping.)
        * a filtered pass skips invariant filing, which is why option (b) above insists on an
          unfiltered one.

      **REQUIRED SEQUENCING FOR OUTBOUND ROWS 2-13 — every one of them is an UPDATE, and an
      UPDATE NEEDS A BINDING THE SCRUB HAS JUST REMOVED.** `outbound_differ.py:518-520` branches on
      `binding_store.get_jira_key(local_id)` and routes `None` to the CREATE path, so a ticket with
      no binding is never updated. Since the scrub deliberately strips every binding from the copied
      store, an outbound edit cell that just mutates a local ticket would CREATE a new DC issue —
      and then its oracle (`fields.summary` on 'the' DC issue) would happily pass against that
      freshly-created issue instead of the one the cell meant to change. Green, and proving nothing:
      the exact failure shape this story exists to end.
      So rows 2-13 (and outbound row 14) share ONE fixture, `bound_dc_issue(...)`, which:

            reason is easy to miss: there is NO inbound-only mode. Every writing mode
            (`bootstrap-strict`, `bootstrap-throttle`, `live`) also runs the OUTBOUND differ,
            so an unscoped pass over the scrubbed store would route its ~10^3 unbound tickets
            down the CREATE path — `bootstrap-strict` (cap=10, `mode.py:106`) would file 10

        (3) returns `(local_id, dc_key)`.

      dependent cell would fall back to the create path and pass for the wrong reason.

      WRITING-MODE inbound pass so the local ticket and its binding are established; (3) delete the
      issue in DC; (4) run the `--mode dry-run` pass and assert the probe entry. Skipping step 2
      leaves no binding, the differ emits nothing, and the jq assertion fails for a reason that has
      nothing to do with the absence path — a false red that would read as a product defect.

- [ ] the effective server page size is OBSERVED and reported in the run output, not assumed, and the
      suite seeds at least `2 * observed + 1` issues IN THE HARNESS so at least three pages are
      required — pagination is a remote-side property and the store copy does not exercise it.
      **HOW TO SEED, and what 'fully recovered' counts.** Seed via `dc_transport.create_issue` in
      a pytest fixture (the same call the existing live cells use — not a raw REST POST, so the
      seeding path is one the adapter actually supports), collecting the returned keys into a
      `seeded_keys` set. **This cell uses an UNFILTERED `--mode dry-run` pass — it is the one
      place a whole-store pass is required, and dry-run is what makes that safe.** Pagination is
      a property of the FETCH crossing page boundaries, so a filtered pass would scope to one id,
      never cross a boundary, and defeat the cell entirely; but an unfiltered WRITING pass would
      run the outbound differ over the scrubbed store and file spurious issues (see the scoping
      note above). Dry-run fetches every page and computes the plan while writing nothing, which
      is exactly what this criterion needs.
      `recovered_count` is therefore read from the PLAN, not from created tickets: the number of
      `seeded_keys` that appear as an inbound create entry in the envelope —
      `jq '[.plan[] | select(.direction == "inbound" and .action == "create")] | .[].local_id'`
      intersected with `{_jira_key_to_local_id(k) for k in seeded_keys}` — and the assertion is
      `recovered_count == len(seeded_keys)`. Counting recovered keys rather than total local
      tickets is deliberate: the store copy already contains unrelated tickets, so a total-count
      assertion would be satisfied by the copy alone and would pass under exactly the truncation
      this criterion exists to catch.
      **SETTLE THE INDEX BEFORE ASSERTING — this criterion is otherwise flaky for the very reason
      [rebar:21fc-51d7-90ca-4a03] existed.** The inbound pass finds issues through `fetcher._iter_pages`
      -> `client.search_issues`, a JQL search, and Jira's Lucene index is eventually consistent, so
      freshly seeded issues may not be searchable yet. A pass run immediately after seeding can
      therefore recover fewer than it should and fail with a TRUNCATION signature that is really
      index lag — the exact confusion that would send the next reader after a pagination bug that
      is not there. So the fixture must POLL the search until it returns all `seeded_keys` (with a
      bounded timeout that FAILS LOUDLY naming index lag) BEFORE the pass runs, and the cell must
      assert that precondition was met rather than assuming it.
